AJK.name: Juneau
AJK.excerpt: Confidence is high on cold air moving in at the surface Monday, along with moisture timing Tuesday and Wednesday. Largest uncertainty is how warm will the incoming airmass be and how quickly we can scrub out any persistent cold air at the surface.

sections.name: Evening, Aviation, And Long Term Forecast Update
paragraphs: No major changes to ongoing forecast this evening. Winds remain light widespread across the panhandle and inner channels, strongest being Eldred Rock northerly around 10 to 15kts. With a weakening system pushing inland, ceilings remain low across much of the panhandle, with areas of patchy fog possible into the early morning hours for any areas that see the slightest bit of clearing. Otherwise, relatively benign, but wet conditions continue. A weak front pushes into the panhandle Friday morning followed up by a stronger, more seasonal front into the panhandle by Friday night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: /Sunday through Wednesday/... Sunday continues to look like one fine day across Southeast, with the potential for some fog development. Stay tuned. Mariners moving around the inner channels should be aware of outflow winds, especially overnight into Monday as high pressure builds across the Yukon and BC provinces. One impact from outflow will be cold air once again infiltrating the Panhandle, especially those closest to the Coast Range and major river inlets, priming us for snow. Expect a large system to move in off the Bering Monday steering plenty of moisture into our area Tuesday into Wednesday. Snow impacts will be directly tied to how prolific the outflow event is for the start of next week, the resulting cold air infiltration, and how quickly relatively warmer southerlies can scrub out the cold airmass at the surface. For now, the published forecast reflects minor snow for some communities separate from Haines and Skagway. It certainly feels like the first snow event for us humble few in Southeast; however, accumulating snow (outside of the Haines and Klondike highways) looks modest, likely only some flakes to perhaps an inch before turning to rain. Yakutat will also see some snow Tuesday. Stay tuned as we monitor for developments thru the weekend.

Confidence is high on cold air moving in at the surface Monday, along with moisture timing Tuesday and Wednesday. Largest uncertainty is how warm will the incoming airmass be and how quickly we can scrub out any persistent cold air at the surface. While it looks like a decent overrunning setup, the limiting factor is the duration of the Monday outflow, limiting snow potential.

sections.name: Prev Discussion
paragraphs: ...ISSUED AT 345 PM AKST Thu Nov 26 2026...
- Continued periods of light rain for Icy Strait Corridor and southward for Thanksgiving and Friday.
- Another system moves in for Friday night into Saturday, bringing slightly increased winds and more rain from Yakutat to around Sumner Strait.
- Drier and cooler weather for Sunday with fog chances for Saturday into Sunday.

Somewhat more benign forecast for Thanksgiving and going into this weekend. The weakening low moving up from the south is converting into an open wave trough, with a bulk of the upper air support far south of the panhandle. What is left is a broad hole of divergence, which is helping keep rain in the forecast for a majority of the panhandle. While plenty of moisture is available, available lift and weak winds in the lower levels does not look to bring any rainfall intensities higher than moderate, except for possibly the extreme southern panhandle during the evening hours.

Going into Friday morning, stronger cold air advection and just enough frontogensis looks to bring a weak, lower level trough to move over the panhandle from NW to SE, once again increases those rain chances. In its wake, a stronger through will sweep across the gulf waters, Friday night and into Saturday morning, weakening around the Yakutat area. Looking to see Yakutat get a bulk of the rainfall, less than a half inch, with the Icy Strait down to Sumner Strait having the highest likelihood to see measurable precip to roughly a quarter inch precipitation. Haines, Skagway, and the highways are not expected to receive much precipitation at this time, as stronger westerly to southwesterly winds are expected to shadow over the Chilkat Range. If any areas does see some snow accumulation, less than 2 inches, it would be on the Klondike Highway.

MARINE... Outer Waters: Overall offshore NE flow is expected to decrease and shift to the west late Thursday night and increase to about 15-20kts as a weak front moves up from the south into early Friday morning. Winds are expected to peak Friday afternoon before diminishing slightly, 10-15kts ahead of another front. Winds shift to the south late Friday as another front approaches the gulf. Winds are not anticipated to build much more than 15-20kts as this secondary front approaches. Behind the front on Saturday morning, winds then shift to the northwest as high pressure builds into the area.

Inner Channels: Conditions across the inner channels are generally settling with Lynn Canal and Stephens Passage remaining elevated around 15kts. Through the evening, these conditions are expected to become less than 10kts. By Friday morning, a shift in pattern brings south to southeast winds as a front approaches from the south. This front is likely to bring elevated winds up to 20kts mainly across southern inner channels, especially east/west oriented channels. Winds are expected to peak last Friday night before diminishing. Winds across the northern panhandle build Friday night as another front moves across the area, especially in north/south oriented channels. Overall, winds diminish again through the day Saturday as high pressure moves into the gulf.

BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Progressive pattern will continue across the north Pacific into the northwestern US, maintaining mild and relatively moist conditions through the period.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Periods of valley rain and mountain snow through Friday, with warm temperatures raising snow levels to 6500-8500 feet.
- Gusty winds in southern areas and brief heavy rain with cold frontal passage Friday night into Saturday morning.
- Unsettled pattern continues with above normal temperatures through next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Looking at a wet and relatively mild next 24-36 hours as westerly flow continues to steer an atmospheric river into the Pac NW. Strong westerly flow aloft (30-50 mph ~10kft MSL) and deep Pacific moisture (PW values ~95th percentile) will support periods of mtn rain/snow across e-central Oregon and w-central Idaho through Friday. Light precipitation will extend into the lower Snake Plain and northern Harney and Malheur counties at times, but any measurable amounts will be less than a tenth of an inch through Friday afternoon. Further south/east, mostly dry conditions will carry through Friday to include the western Magic Valley. Snow levels will range from around 6.5kft over e-central Oregon and w-central Idaho mtns to 8-9kft MSL in the southern Boise/Soldier mtns. Above the snowline, accumulation of 3-6 inches is expected through Friday afternoon with upwards of 8 inches along western aspects.

Friday night will see a shortwave trough and accompanying cold front push across the area, extending the chance of precipitation to the northern NV border. The combination of mid- level dynamics and accompanying wind max will enhance precipitation rates, especially in the mtns. Snow levels will fall to 5-8kft MSL by Saturday morning. The heavier snowfall stays above 6500 feet, but light amounts are possible down to 5-5.5kft as the precipitation ends early Saturday. Elevations where it stays all snow (above 7.5-8kft) snow totals of 8-14 inches are expected.

Along with an increased chance of precipitation, the frontal passage will ramp up winds across SE Oregon and the areas for SW Idaho from the Snake Plain to the NV border Friday night. Gusts will mostly peak between 25-40 mph. Usually windier locations around Steens Mtn, Snake Plain and higher terrain along the NV border could see gusts up to 50 mph.

The precipitation scatters out on Saturday morning as the low exits to the east. Most areas dry out by afternoon while the southern mtns keep a 10-20% chance of showers. High temperatures will run 3-6 degrees cooler than Friday, the lower Snake Plain being the exception where improved post frontal mixing will mix out an inversion and warm temperatures. A 10-20% chance of showers continues in the mtns Saturday night as a warm front lifts into the area.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Progressive pattern will continue across the north Pacific into the northwestern US, maintaining mild and relatively moist conditions through the period. Several Pacific storms are forecast to move inland, with the first one leaving our area Monday, the next one Tuesday night/Wednesday passing to our south but close enough to affect our southern zones, then a third one into all zones late Thursday. We see no sign of northerly flow aloft that could bring cold air into our area, but rather a continuation of westerly flow, keeping temperatures around 10 degrees above normal.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: While models still indicate a weakening trough to impact the area by Wednesday or Thursday, the latest runs hinted at a weak closed low structure remaining in tact and also tracking a bit further northward.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Hazardous travel Friday night - Saturday evening for the northern mountains and I-70 mountain corridor due to snow and blowing snow. Local snowfall amounts greater than 12" possible.

- Banded rain/snow for the the plains and I-25 Corridor Saturday to Saturday evening. Brief heavy snow with generally light accumulations possible, including potential for Denver's first measurable snowfall of the season.
- Gusty winds expected along the northern Front Range and northern border area Friday, spreading to all the plains Saturday.
- Return of mostly dry weather Sunday - Tuesday, next disturbance may arrive by Wednesday or Thursday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Mild Thanksgiving weather will be replaced by unsettled weather Friday night and Saturday which will affect post holiday travel plans.

In the meantime, tonight will feature dry conditions with only passing high clouds. Temperatures will settle closer to normal overnight lows once again. Friday is still on track to bring increasing winds to the Front Range and northern plains as the upper level ridge over us today breaks down and a stronger zonal flow develops across the Central Rockies. That means a return of gusty winds to the higher foothills and mountains, with gusts of 45-60 mph above timberline and higher wind prone areas. Ingredients like stability and increasing forward shear do not favor significant mountain wave amplification, so we think those higher wind gusts should stay out of the adjacent plains. That said, it will still be breezy in some of the local favored downslope areas like Highway 93, while daytime mixing also supports locations closer to the Wyoming border getting breezy with gusts of 30-35 mph in the late morning and afternoon. We'll introduce the first chance of snow to the northern mountains through the day as mid level moisture is now forecast to increase sufficiently for light snow showers, mainly north of Rabbit Ears Pass.

The main focus shifts to Friday night and Saturday as a fast moving shortwave drives through the Central Rockies in strong west/northwest flow aloft. As discussed last night, models remain in good agreement with this feature. However, most have sped up this disturbance by a few hours and not surprisingly as we're in such strong zonal flow. This means snow will start in earnest across the northern mountains Friday night. We'll first see this more significant snowfall develop in the northern tier of mountains where westerly orographic flow is more favorable and moisture is deeper, but even the I-70 Corridor should start to get into the heavier snow after midnight tomorrow night as large scale QG ascent occurs ahead of the shortwave and in the left exit region of a 120 kt jet. Those favorable features, along with passage of a mid level front and brief but rather pronounced frontogenesis, will support snow through the day Saturday. In fact, it's not impossible that we see a brief period of very heavy snow or snow squalls with the frontal passage in the late morning to early afternoon hours. We'll continue to message avoiding post-Thanksgiving travel on Saturday through the high country if possible. The earlier start also supports more snowfall, backed up by the latest uptick in ensemble and operational guidance. That suggests the northern tier of mountains get 8-14" with the I-70 mountain corridor and Summit County now in the 5-10" range. That puts us on the higher end of Winter Weather Advisory Criteria. If trends continue, then we'll likely have to upgrade the northern tier of mountain zones to a Winter Storm Warning since they'll be beneficiaries of the earlier start.

Now, back down to the I-25 Corridor and plains...The instability and favorable ingredients mentioned above will also be conducive to showers spreading off the higher terrain through the day. With the earlier frontal passage, we've also trimmed forecast temperatures with anywhere north of Denver likely not getting out of the 40s before the frontal passage. The entire forecast area will see temperatures drop with the frontal passage as it sweeps quickly southward across the plains. It may arrive as early as mid morning especially as trends continue with the faster shortwave. And, it should be noted we expect quite the blast of northerly wind across all of the plains with near high wind criteria being met during and shortly after the frontal passage. Widespread gusts to 40-55 mph are expected at this point, with a 10-20% chance of gusts >58 mph (high wind criteria) east of I-25. Now, back to precip...an earlier frontal arrival would mean a higher chance that the synoptic scale lift and shallow anticyclonic upslope behind the front would be able to join forces. Thus, we've bumped precipitation chances further for Saturday afternoon especially over and south of metro Denver (more favored in N-NNE flow). Temperatures will also be turning colder more quickly, which supports more snow vs rain and a growing chance (50-60%) of our first official measurable snow for Denver. With the strong F-gen and mid level instability, we can't rule out bands of heavier snow as well with localized amounts of 1-3" or more (favoring south metro into the foothills west and southwest of Denver). Any heavier bands could also result in brief slush accumulation on roads, with propensity for greater impacts in the colder foothills and Palmer Divide should the heavier snow bands develop there.

We do expect snow to taper off fairly quickly Saturday evening as the system is now trending faster, but some travel impacts may linger in the mountains into early Sunday morning due to residual road snow. Those conditions will improve rather quickly however with return of sunshine, so Sunday is shaping up to be a much better post-holiday travel day than Saturday.

Mainly dry weather will then persist into Monday and Tuesday, although the flow appears to become zonal enough to have a chance of light snow showers for the high country. After a chilly Sunday, temperatures will be warming back to above normal levels both days.

While models still indicate a weakening trough to impact the area by Wednesday or Thursday, the latest runs hinted at a weak closed low structure remaining in tact and also tracking a bit further northward. This will mean another chance of rain/snow showers for the forecast area with temperatures cooling to near normal levels again.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Sunday will start off chilly as skies clear overnight behind Saturday's system. Despite more sunshine, we will still have a cold airmass in place, which should keep highs down in the upper 30s to lower 40s.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Winds will increase this evening through Friday night with gusts peaking to 65-70 mph at the wind-prone locations. Heavy mountain snow is expected Friday night into Saturday where gusty winds will persist.
- A strong cold front will sweep through the area Saturday morning, bringing colder temperatures and snow.
- Saturday's snowfall may be locally heavy, with reduced visibility in falling and blowing snow and minor accumulations impacting holiday travel.
- Another round of strong winds is possible (50% chance) in the wind prone areas Sunday through early Tuesday

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A beautiful and mild Thanksgiving day today, with temperatures soaring into the mid to upper 50s along and east of the I-25 corridor this afternoon, which is around 5-10 degrees above average for this time of year. It is also quite breezy out, mainly along the I-80 corridor where some gusts as high as 45-50 mph have occurred at the wind-prone areas. Combined with RH values dropping to 8-14% this afternoon mainly across southern portions of Laramie County, any outdoor burning is not recommended. These Red Flag Conditions are expected to be relatively short-lived and localized this afternoon, so decided against issuing any fire weather highlights. Current visible satellite imagery shows some mid and high level clouds spreading across the area from an atmospheric river located over the east-central Pacific. These are being transported over the region by a 120-130 knot 300 mb jet located over the Pacific Northwest, which will bring us a wetter and more active pattern as we head into this upcoming weekend.

In the short term, the main headline will be high wind conditions, mainly for the wind-prone areas along and downwind of the Laramie Range (looking at you, Bordeaux), along with the usual high wind hot spots located along the I-80 corridor. Expect these winds to ramp up as we head into the evening hours and continue through tomorrow morning as zonal 700 mb flow increases to 55-65 knots overnight. These higher winds aloft are in response to a weak open wave digging across Alberta and Saskatchewan to our north, increasing the height gradient over the Intermountain West. Omega fields overnight into Friday morning show mountain wave signatures, with model cross- sections continuing to show strong static stability at mountain-top, all of which signal a downsloping wind event with the potent cross- barrier flow. With further support from in-house guidance which currently shows 60-80% probabilities of high wind conditions for Arlington starting tonight and carrying into early Saturday morning and Bordeaux with 40-60% probabilities ending some time mid-morning Friday, continued the High Wind Warnings for these areas. High wind conditions for Cheyenne look much less probable (~20%) on Friday, though it will still be a blustery day with some isolated gusts up to 55 mph not out of the question depending on where the mountain wave breaks. Also decided to issue a High Wind Watch for primarily the northern half of Carbon County (including Rawlins) starting late tomorrow afternoon and lasting through Saturday morning underneath the 60+ knot 700 mb flow. However, confidence is lower that high wind conditions will occur in places like Rawlins where current guidance shows the strongest downward omega primarily south of I-80.

Now is the time we can finally (!) talk about some moisture across SE Wyoming, primarily for the Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges through Saturday Morning. After a mild, but breezy day Friday with above- average temperatures expected, a 115-120 knot jet streak will dig south and east into the Four Corners Region in sync with a slightly weaker 100 knot jet located to our north over Montana and the Dakotas. This is generally a favorable pattern for large-scale ascent as SE Wyoming will be influenced by this coupled jet structure, resting in the left-exit region of the southern speed maximum and in the right-entrance region of the northern jet streak. Within the short-term period, the highest QPF will be confined to the Sierra Madre Range and especially the Snowy Range under WNW flow aloft. While the heaviest snow totals will likely remain above 9000 feet, did go ahead and issue a Winter Storm Warning for the Snowy Range where there is the highest confidence in 12+ inch totals is expected. Given the orientation of the flow relative to the Sierra Madre Range, kept snow totals below warning criteria as accumulation is expected to remain below a foot. Generally, expecting most of the precipitation to be orographically-driven overnight Friday into early Saturday with locations along and east of the I-25 corridor remaining mostly dry as winds will remain out of the west and downsloping off the Laramie Range.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: An active and dynamic day is expected across the area on Saturday as a quick hitting storm system sweeps through the region. The synoptic setup will be driven by a potent upper level shortwave riding along the strong upper level jet stream. This will be carrying with it a sharp surface cold front which will drive major weather changes through the area on Saturday. The main change with today's update is a considerable acceleration in the timing of the frontal passage. Most of the latest suite of model guidance has the frontal boundary fully through the area by 10-11AM on Saturday (with the notable exception of the RRFS). A morning passage will mean that we won't quite see as distinct of a temperature drop, but expect a fairly sudden wind shift and small temperature drop, but this will really hold down Saturday's high temperature forecast. If the front indeed passes through in the morning hours, most areas will not exceed 40 degrees on Saturday. Behind the front, expect winds to remain strong and gusty, but the threat for high winds will evaporate quickly after an hour or so behind the front.

This system is also looking increasingly likely to bring the first widespread snow event of the season. Accumulation totals are not expected to be significant (outside of the mountains) due to the quick hitting nature of the event, but that doesn't necessarily mean no impacts. The primary lifting mechanism appears to be vorticity advection ahead of the shortwave trough axis, favorable jet streak dynamics (we are under the left exit region), and powerful frontogenesis sweeping through along the frontal boundary. In addition, models show very rapid surface pressure increases behind the front on the order of 2-4 mb per hour with some minimal convective instability thanks to steep lapse rates. The character appears likely to be banded snowfall, with locally heavy rates underneath, but it shouldn't last very long. Rates could be 1-2" per hour underneath the heaviest bands of snow, with some potential to reach snow squall criteria. Snow squall parameters are around 2 to 4, largely limited by the weak instability. With the acceleration in the timing today, the primary period of concern actually now appears to be Saturday morning through the early or perhaps mid afternoon. Some snow shower activity should linger through the afternoon and into the early evening hours, as dry air will not be very abrupt to work into the area behind the system, but all activity should be done by the late evening hours. Most areas outside of the mountains should see around a dusting to an inch or so of snow, though the lowest elevations of the North Platte River Valley may not receive any. There is potential for amounts in the 1-3" range generally along the US-20 corridor and near Laramie where frontogenesis lingers for longer combined with favorable orographic lift into the Pine Ridge or southern Laramie Range.

Sunday will start off chilly as skies clear overnight behind Saturday's system. Despite more sunshine, we will still have a cold airmass in place, which should keep highs down in the upper 30s to lower 40s. The flow aloft will start to turn more zonal Sunday onwards, which will increase the potential for strong winds in the wind prone areas once again. 700-mb height gradients are marginally supportive for high winds in the Arlington/Elk Mountain area during the day on Sunday, spreading eastward to the Laramie range wind prone areas Sunday night into Monday as surface pressure falls east of the range. Current probabilities are around 60 to 70% for the Arlington area, and 50% for the I-80 Summit and Bordeaux areas. Elsewhere, westerly flow will resume warm air advection as 700-mb temperatures climb back above 0C Monday and remain there through at least Wednesday. This should push highs back to around 5-10F above seasonal averages. Conditions look largely dry, though there may be another round of light mountain snow around Monday into Tuesday with a weak shortwave passing through.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Snow showers will taper off Sunday morning, with only a few orographically driven showers lingering along the Park Range under drying northwesterly flow. A transient ridge builds in Sunday into Monday, bringing quieter conditions seasonably mild temperatures.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow will begin along the northern Divide late Friday, lingering through Sunday morning. Snow totals of 10-14 inches are expected for the Park and Elkhead mountains, with 4-8 inches across the Flat Tops and Central Divide Mountains.
- Winds gusting up to 45 mph are expected with this evening, leading to blowing and drifting snow and difficult driving conditions over the mountain passes.
- An unsettled pattern looks to continue into next week with potential for more mountain snow, but details remain uncertain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The ridge to our west is in the process of breaking down this evening, with increasing upper level moisture in the form of mid to high level clouds spilling in from the northwest. Aside from the clouds, seasonably mild temperatures and relatively quiet conditions will continue through the day Friday.

The first in a series of shortwaves in the northwesterly flow reaches eastern Utah and western Colorado Friday evening. Light snow showers are expected to begin along the Northern Divide and spread south through the night. The strongest in this series of waves arrives Saturday morning, with the highest snowfall rates expected between 5AM and 5PM Saturday. This will impact morning and evening commutes, as well as any post-Thanksgiving Holiday traffic over the mountain passes. A Winter Storm Warning has been issued for the Park and Elkhead mountains, and Winter Weather Advisories remain in effect for the Central Divide mountains and Flat Tops, all from 5PM Friday evening to 5AM Sunday morning. For the Park and Elkhead mountains, 10-14 inches of snow are expected, with locally higher amounts possible. For the Central Divide Mountains and the Flat Tops, snow totals of 4-8 inches are expected, with locally higher amounts possible. This system will also bring strong northwesterly winds capable of gusting to 45 mph. As a result, blowing and drifting snow will also be a concern. If planning on travelling at any point on Saturday, be prepared for difficult winter driving conditions, with blowing snow reducing visibility and slick, messy road conditions.

Snow showers will taper off Sunday morning, with only a few orographically driven showers lingering along the Park Range under drying northwesterly flow. A transient ridge builds in Sunday into Monday, bringing quieter conditions seasonably mild temperatures. This ridge flattens through the day Monday, with flow shifting from northwesterly to more zonal in response to a wave moving into the Pacific Northwest. Model confidence with the impact of this first wave remains low, however it is possible that increasing moisture and favorable orographics will result in some light snow showers along the Divide. Blended guidance has reasonably high probabilities (50-70%) of an inch or two of snow with this first wave. Looking towards the middle of the week, there is potential for a stronger, more southerly system to impact the Four Corners and southern mountains. Model guidance remains in relatively poor agreement, with significant spread. The southerly track does increase potential for atmospheric river moisture to accompany this system. However, the exact track of this system can make the difference between a solid mountain snowfall and seeing no snow at all. We shall have to wait and see how the forecast for this system develops over the coming days.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Guidance shows another disturbance is fcst to move through. However the brunt of the energy on latest 12Z guidance is showing most of the forcing will move across N New Mexico, so best chances of precip will likely occur along and south of US50. \/Hodanish

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - NW impulse will bring wind driven snow to the central mtns Saturday; with some possible pocket of snow on the plains Sat night.
- Warm Saturday, much cooler Sunday Plains.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Tonight...Dry, and a bit warmer than last night. Banana belt areas will be in the M30s to L40s while eastern plains will be U20s to L30s. San Luis Valley will be mainly in the L20s. High clouds will be on the increase.

Tomorrow...Lee troughing will set up over the plains in advance of a potent short wave in the developing NW'erly flow aloft. Quite a bit of high cloudiness likely. Temps will max out in the U60s mtns/plains interface with M60s eastern plains. Valleys will see 50s.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Potent disturbance in the NW Flow will move across the region. This will some accumulating snow to the central mtns. Additionally, it will bring increasing winds to all of the higher terrain.

Heaviest snow will fall on Saturday over the central mtns. Winds of 50 to 60 mph will be likely so travel in the central mtns will be difficult. Overall snow amounts are expected to be modest, with 4 to 6 inches likely. most of the snow over the central mtns will fall north of Cottonwood Pass.
The San Luis Valley and SW mtns should remain dry Saturday but it will be windy.

As for the plains, Saturday will be mild and breezy. The front should cross the region during mid afternoon time period with strong northerly gusts likely by later in teh day. Winds of 45 to 55 mph will be likely. We may see some gusts reaching high wind criteria late afternoon/evening over the far eastern plains.

As for precip on the plains, we will likely see rain/snow over the Palmer Divide by late morning into the evening hours. Some of this precip will be possible over the southern I-25 corridor region by evening. Some guidance members show some light showers over the far eastern plains.
Much cooler all areas. Max temps will likely only be in the 40s to around 50 over the plains and larger valleys, but it will be dry. Winds all areas will be significantly less than Saturday.
Dry most areas with milder temps returning. The only area which we may see some shower will be over the central mtns where some snow showers will be possible.

Guidance shows another disturbance is fcst to move through. However the brunt of the energy on latest 12Z guidance is showing most of the forcing will move across N New Mexico, so best chances of precip will likely occur along and south of US50. \/Hodanish

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Beyond this system, there is medium confidence that this wavetrain continues through the first to second week of December.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Temperatures will be increasingly mild for Friday, with maxes around 5-10F above seasonal normals.
- A weak storm system will move across northern Utah late Friday into Saturday, bringing generally light valley rain and mountain snow to northern Utah and southwest Wyoming.

- Dry conditions will return temporarily on Sunday, with a more active pattern resuming into the middle of the week. A potent area of low pressure looks to make impacts primarily across southern Utah, bringing high elevation snowfall and valley rain.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A weak area of high pressure remains steadfast over the region and will continue to do so through the next 24-hours. This area of high pressure will gradually weaken throughout the day on Friday, with weak shortwave impulses ushering in cooler air overhead. This decrease in temperatures overhead looks to aid in better mixing across the region, which will help to bring an increase in temperatures as valley inversions weaken. Increased moisture overhead from an active northern stream will also allow for increased cloud cover through the day on Friday.

This moisture, tied to an upstream atmospheric river, will continue to increase through Friday evening/ Saturday morning as the parent shortwave trough moves into the region. The existing inland-pentrating atmospheric river will weaken as the parent shortwave energy moves into northern Utah early Saturday morning. That said, the anomalous moisture will pair with the shortwave trough and interact with the high terrain in northern Utah to generate a period of high elevation snowfall and valley rain from roughly Salt Lake/ Tooele County northward. Depending on the overall depth of the trough, we could see precipitation extend as far south as the I-70 corridor (primarily in the high terrain), but the expected limited impacts will exist north of the I-80 corridor. Again, while impacts will be limited, a brief period of moderate high elevation snowfall and low elevation (<6,800ft) rain should be anticipated in the Bear River mountains and Ogden area mountains early Saturday morning. No headlines are expected to be issued at this time.

A brief period of ridging will round out the weekend, bringing stable conditions areawide on Sunday with mild temperatures expected throughout Utah and southwest Wyoming. Largely dry conditions will prevail through at least Tuesday morning across much of the area with the exception of the northern Bear Rivers. The aforementioned active northern stream looks to bring another round of light precipitation to this area from Monday afternoon through early Tuesday.

Focus of the forecast period will then shift to the Tuesday/Wednesday/Thursday timeframe as the persistent ridge we've been dealing with begins to break down, opening the door to much more potent areas of low pressure. Ensemble guidance is in fairly good agreement on a deep area of low pressure moving in from the eastern Pacific, tracking into the southwestern U.S. (textbook El Nino) from Tuesday through Thursday. While the ensemble means from the EPS and GEFS are in generally good agreement, there still exists a fairly high amount of spread when breaking down and clustering individual members. The biggest uncertainty at this time is figuring out how far south/north the low will pass... a farther northern track will allow for much more widespread valley rain and mountain snow (45% chance), whereas a more southern track (in line with ensemble means) would favor primary precipitation concerns across the southern half of Utah (55% chance). While odds are generally split, southern Utah still looks to fare better with precipitation totals from this system but the forecast spread remains high.

Beyond this system, there is medium confidence that this wavetrain continues through the first to second week of December. We'll need to see how things evolve throughout the week, but there looks to be a non-zero chance that we'll see our first decent chance at widespread lower elevation snowfall across Utah around December 6-8... something to keep and eye on!

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Near and above treeline, you can trigger an avalanche that is large enough to injure and bury you. Slopes that face the north half of the compass, and are steeper than about 30 degrees are the most suspect. Give slopes where recent storms drifted snow a wide berth; you might trigger them from above, next to, or below.
Seek out wind-sheltered areas and slopes below treeline for safer travel options.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: You can trigger a dangerous avalanche where you encounter older wind-drifted slabs below ridgelines, especially on northwest through north to east-facing slopes at upper elevations. You might trigger them from thin spots above, adjacent to, or below the drifted features. Choose wind-sheltered terrain to avoid the problem.
At this point, Saturday's storm does not look to raise the danger for this area. However, if the storm tracks further south it might. Check back Friday evening for a forecast update.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches due to thin and discontinuous snow cover. You can trigger a small avalanche in wind-drifted snow above treeline. Look for these drifts below ridges and around rocky outcrops on slopes facing west through north to east.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Elevations above 7,000 feet have 1-2 feet of snow on the ground. You may encounter pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north- and east-facing terrain. If the snow feels stiff or slabby underfoot, then find a different aspect away from wind-drifted snow. The biggest hazard remains thin snow cover and hitting rocks, logs, and stumps. Even a small slide through thin coverage could end a season before it even starts.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: Above 7,000 feet, a layered snowpack is beginning to build for the season. Good, albeit thin, skiing and riding conditions have been reported at upper elevations. Elevations below 7,000 feet remain thin and bony. Before November 13th, most slopes were bare. Winter trailhead access remains a challenge as there is not quite enough snow to launch sleds. Most forest roads become impassable by vehicle above 6,500 feet. As folks start poking around the mountains, remember that avalanches can occur with just a few feet of snow on the ground. There may be some lingering pockets of wind slabs above 7,500 feet on north and east-facing terrain features, particularly just below ridgelines.

Beginning Thanksgiving Day, a large storm system will impact the Pacific and Interior Northwest. Strong winds, mountain snow, and fluctuating rain/snow levels will be in the cards for several days. Pay attention to changing weather and snow conditions heading into the weekend. Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

Fresh wind slabs will come back onto the menu with more snow and wind later this week. Pay attention to gullies that can become crossloaded and may also act as a terrain trap. Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices. Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
Turn On Your Snow and Avalanche Brain

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).

• Help us paint a picture of what's going on in the mountains. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps forecasters and the public alike.
